sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

Introduction We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered. Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson Computer-use agents (CUAs) carry out tasks by observing and acting on digital environments. Their interfaces determine what they can observe and which operations they can request. Current computeruse frameworks focus on GUI interaction, supplemented by dedicated tools (Xie et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). These interfaces are designed by humans and fixed before task execution. Even though these interfaces are built specifically for agents, they still depend on human judgments about what those agents need. This practice creates three problems for computer-use. First, it ties progress to manual labor. Computer use is open-ended, and each new family of tasks or model release exposes new failure modes. human researcher must read trajectories, diagnose failures, and use them to write new primitives, observation formats, or memory mechanisms, and then release the result as new agent framework with new preset interface. This loop does not scale with task diversity. Second, static interface often mismatches the task, and current methods compensate with test-time compute instead of better interface. For example, an agent may complete shell task by clicking to open terminal window, typing commands one character at time, and reading screenshots of partly occluded terminal for feedback, when direct shell interface would be faster and more reliable (Jia et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2026). Additional sampling can raise benchmark scores under such mismatches, but through wasteful and brittle strategies. Third, methods that compose test-time experience into reusable skills or routines inherit the same limit (Agashe et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b). Each skill is composition of the preset observations and actions. Distillation can reorder what the interface allows, but it cannot extend it. These problems arise because the interface is treated as design decision that humans make before deployment, and not as an object that can be studied and improved from the agents own experience. Instead, computer-use interfaces should evolve from the agents own experience. Therefore, we introduce Agent S41 an autonomous CUA scientist that studies computer-use agents and builds Evolving Agent Interfaces through populationbased evolution. Its output is repository of mixed interfaces and knowledge about when and how to use them. The task agents model and harness remain fixed, with the harness governing model invocation, execution, permissions, and task budgets. The task agent uses candidate repositories of Evolving Agent Interfaces to attempt synthetic tasks, producing trajectories without groundtruth success labels. meta-agent studies these trajectories and forms hypotheses about how changes to actions, observations, or usage knowledge could help the task agent. It conFigure 2 With Evolving Agent Interfaces built by Agent S4, Qwen3.8-27B exceeds GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 in binary success on the challenging OSWorld V2 benchmark at small fraction of their cost. 1The name reads as Agent Scientist for (4) Evolving Agent Interfaces 2 Evolving Agent Interfaces structs descendants through mutation of one repository or crossover between two. Descendants can add, revise, or remove interfaces and knowledge, and the population retains alternative designs for further development and recombination. To limit specialization to the tasks that motivated these changes, Agent S4 separates the evidence used for construction from that used for selection. The meta-agent receives training trajectories, while validation instructions, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain hidden from it. Validation performance guides parent selection. We evaluate the final selected repository on the full benchmark. The meta-agent never observes any benchmark task while constructing interfaces, and the validation tasks influence only which repositories are selected during evolution. We evaluate Agent S4 on OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026) and ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025). On the full 108-task OSWorld V2 set, Qwen3.8-27B with the evolved repository reaches 21.3% binary success, above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%) at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. In separate evolution run on ScienceBoard, which covers niche scientific applications, the evolved repository reaches 58.6% success rate, compared with 41.4% for the human-designed interface of Qwen CUA. These results show that agents can evolve their own computer-use interfaces from purely synthetic, verifier-free task experience and outperform human-designed interfaces. We compare our setup against evolutionary baselines such as linear evolution and measure the effect of giving the meta-agent scratch virtual machine to test its evolved interfaces. Finally, we qualitatively compare agents that act through evolved interfaces with agents that use fixed, human-designed interfaces. Our contributions are: Evolving Agent Interfaces from synthetic, verifier-free experience. We introduce Agent S4, which evolves repository of interfaces and usage knowledge from synthetic task experience, without success labels or task verifiers, while the task agents model and harness stay fixed. Validation tasks the meta-agent never sees decide which repositories to develop further. Evolving interfaces outperform fixed ones. With repository of interfaces evolved by Agent S4, Qwen3.8-27B exceeds both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 in binary success on OSWorld V2 at small fraction of their cost, and improves ScienceBoard success over fixed-interface agent with the same model. Analysis of evolved interfaces. Repository and trajectory analyses show that evolved interfaces change both what the agent observes and how it acts, across desktop-wide, application-specific, cross-application and task-specific interfaces. We also compare evolution strategies, with and without scratch environment for the meta-agent. 2. The meta-agent observes none of these tasks during construction, and validation tasks drawn from the same benchmark affect only selection. 4. Experimental Setup Benchmarks and task sets. OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026) is our primary benchmark, and ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025) tests generalization to niche scientific computer-use applications and workflows. Repository evolution uses 30 synthetic training tasks for OSWorld V2 and 48 for ScienceBoard, plus 15 official validation tasks for each. Synthetic task attempts yield trajectories without ground-truth success labels. The meta-agent receives these training trajectories. Validation scores guide selection, but validation trajectories and evaluators remain outside its evidence. Fullbenchmark results cover 108 OSWorld V2 and 169 ScienceBoard tasks, including the 15 validation tasks of each. Benchmark details appear in Appendix A, and synthetic task construction is described below and in Appendix D. Model and harness. On both benchmarks, the task agent and meta-agent use Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) in modified Prime Agent harness (Karten et al., 2026) that executes code in persistent IPython kernel, with Medium reasoning, 131,072-token context window, 32,000-token output limit, and automatic context compaction. The model and harness remain fixed within each search. Appendix gives the harness version, sampling parameters, and compaction settings; Appendix gives implementation constraints and builder prompts. Appendix lists the rates and remaining runtime settings. Synthetic task construction. We constructed 30 synthetic tasks for OSWorld V2 and 50 for ScienceBoard, of which 48 are used (Appendix E), giving Agent S4 task experience for evolving Agent Interfaces and usage knowledge without ground-truth success labels. Tasks follow each benchmarks methodology but use independently authored scenarios. For OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026), we studied its task-construction principles and challenge-phenomenon taxonomy, and scaled the reported counts of overlapping phenomena into approximate targets for our 30 tasks. These targets guided the representation of capabilities such as cross-source reasoning, visual-spatial precision, and implicit-state inference. For ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025), we followed planned distribution across six scientific applications and preserved its compact tasks, usually centered on one application and one meaningful outcome. Tasks were created agentically by coordinator (GPT-6 Astra), authors (GPT-5.6-Sol), and independent reviewers (GPT-5.6-Sol). The coordinator tracked accepted tasks against the planned counts and assigned new tasks to phenomena or applications below target. Each author started from fresh context with application documentation, design requirements, and summaries of accepted synthetic tasks, but without access to official task instances, evaluators, or task-agent trajectories. Authors produced instructions, input artifacts, and environment setup specifications, documenting provenance and capability assumptions. Reviewers checked originality, coherence, feasibility, and appropriate complexity. To ensure that no synthetic task overlaps with an existing benchmark task, they compared each candidates purpose, dependencies, operations, and deliverables against official instruction and setup metadata and against the accepted synthetic set. Each claimed challenge had to be supported by the actual materials. The coordinator returned concrete defects for up to two revision rounds, rejected overlapping designs, and kept official comparisons out of author feedback. Automated input and setup checks supplemented these reviews, and only accepted versions entered the training set. No step graded task-agent attempts or produced reference solutions. 5. Evolving interfaces improve the same model. Agents with fixed interfaces already seek programmatic access (Yuan et al., 2026). Terminal commands account for 24.7% of their actions, and GPT-5.5 devotes 78% of its budget to code, API, or file operations (Yuan et al., 2026, Section 4). Under fixed interface, each such program is typed through the desktop and its result is read from screenshot. Acting through agent evolved interfaces removes this indirection, and the evolved repository supplies interfaces for the applications and data that recur across tasks. The additions include ChimeraX command interface, GRASS GIS modules that run in the live session and KAlgebra calculator that evaluates many expressions in one call. The gains are largest on KAlgebra, where success rises from 48% to 68%. These results show that Agent S4 can evolve useful interfaces for specialized scientific software from synthetic training experience. 7. Analysis 7.1. Evolution Dynamics Table 4 Effect of the seed repository and comparison of evolution strategies on the full OSWorld V2 benchmark. All rows use Qwen3.8-27B in Prime Agent. Each evolution row reports the best repository selected by that strategy. Appendix A.2 lists the contents of the seed repository. With scratch VM, the meta-agent can open applications and test interfaces while building the repository. The first two rows of Table 4 show the task agent with no repository and with the seed repository. The seed raises binary success from 15.74% to 19.44% while leaving partial score nearly unchanged (44.93% versus 44.90%), and lowers task-solving cost from $1.36 to $1.11 per task. Evolution without scratch VM then raises binary success to 21.30% and partial score to 46.90% at nearly the same cost ($1.10). The seed therefore provides useful starting point, and evolution improves it on binary success and partial score. Evolution strategies. We compare three ways of evolving the repository. The first is population-based evolution with scratch virtual machine (VM), in which the meta-agent can open applications and test interfaces. The second is population-based evolution without the scratch VM. The third is linear evolution with scratch VM, in which the meta-agent keeps refining each new child repository. With scratch VM, population-based evolution reaches the same binary success as linear evolution (19.44%) and higher partial score (51.06% versus 47.17%). Without scratch VM, population-based evolution reaches the highest binary success (21.30%) but lower partial score (46.90%). The scratch VM therefore improves partial progress, while the best binary success comes from evolution without it. 7.2. Qualitative Study of Evolved Interfaces taxonomy of evolved interfaces. To compare runs, we label each interface by the part of the computer it covers and the purpose it serves. The four labels can overlap: 11 Evolving Agent Interfaces System-wide interfaces cover the desktop and operating system as whole, such as inspecting windows or launching and monitoring background processes. App-specific interfaces expose the objects of one named application, such as spreadsheet ranges in LibreOffice, tracks in REAPER audio project, or molecules in ChimeraX. Cross-App interfaces work on data or platforms shared by many applications, such as reading and rendering PDF files regardless of which application created them, or reading pages on any website. Task-specific interfaces package procedure for particular goal together with check of whether it is achieved, such as checking Lean proof, compiling it, updating the editor and reporting completion. Interfaces also grow after they are introduced, so we label each added operation separately. For example, the office-document interface is App-specific because it edits documents through LibreOffice itself, but an operation added to it later that edits OpenDocument files directly, without the application, is Cross-App. Figure 4 counts new interfaces and these later extensions separately. Table 7 in Appendix B.3 gives examples of evolved interfaces, with what each lets the agent observe and do. Figure 4 Interface discovery and extension across 30 candidates per population run. a, New interfaces (blue): distinct coherent interfaces absent from the seed, labeled by their implemented scope across the run. b, Interface extensions (orange): newly introduced operations first recorded after their interfaces introduction, each labeled independently by its own behavior. On OSWorld V2 without scratch VM, evolution introduces four new interfaces and 127 extensions, including 29 System-wide, 63 App-specific and 40 Cross-App extensions. An interface or extension can carry more than one label, so the counts per label can add up to more than the total. Most of its growth therefore deepens interfaces the agent already has. With scratch VM, where the meta-agent can open applications and test its code, the population introduces 12 new interfaces and 253 extensions. Nine of the new interfaces are App-specific and nine are Cross-App. Seven carry both labels, such as the interfaces for editing musical scores, audio projects and 3D scenes, which operate one application while reading and writing file formats that other applications share. Cross-App extensions rise to 129. These additional application interfaces are likely explanation for the higher partial score of the best repository evolved with scratch VM. On ScienceBoard, evolution introduces seven new interfaces and 91 extensions. Six of the new interfaces and 77 of the extensions are App-specific, for scientific applications such as ChimeraX, KAlgebra, GRASS GIS and Lean. Its three Task-specific extensions package procedures for displaying map in GRASS GIS and completing proof in Lean. 12 Evolving Agent Interfaces Figure 5 Human-curated versus Evolved Interface. Top: the Qwen CUA baseline uses fixed, human-designed interface prioritizing frequent screenshots with mouse and keyboard actions. It reads the receipts and searches the card charges through repeated GUI interactions (steps 21111). Bottom: Prime Agent with the repository evolved by Agent S4. It reads the mailbox and the bank records through the evolved browser interface, whose browser.api sends requests from inside the already logged-in tab and returns the data as text (calls 17 and 44). It fetches the attachments with curl, and reads them with pdftotext. Across all three runs, evolved interfaces let the agent observe the desktop, an applications own objects, data shared across applications, and whether goal has been met, and act on each of these in single call. Evolution therefore widens the range of software the agent can operate and raises the level at which it sees, acts and checks its progress. Case Study: Using the evolved browser interface to handle web data search and fetching instead of fixed interface. Figure 5 follows the information-gathering portion of OSWorld V2 task 008, which requires receipts and corresponding card charges for an expense claim. The fixed-interface Qwen CUA agent opens receipt emails one at time, handles five browser download warnings, and twice tries to open an invoice before its download has finished. Finding the $500 NeurIPS charge also requires eight scrolls and four clicks on Load more. With the evolved repository, the task agent uses browser.api to retrieve mailbox contents and attachment URLs as structured data. It downloads three PDFs with curl, reads them with pdftotext, and reuses the browser interface to query the bank dashboard and cross-check the charges. The agent combines reusable browser interface with existing command-line tools to gather evidence across applications, reducing repeated visual Evolving Agent Interfaces navigation and manual download handling. Appendix B.5 provides the more illustrated examples of agents benefitting from using an evolved interface for applications like MailHub, XMind, Zotero, ReviewSphere, and Word tracked changes. 7.3. Repeated Validation during Evolution Long-horizon computer-use tasks show substantial runto-run variance (Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026), so single validation run can overrate repository. On ScienceBoard, we therefore re-evaluate the three highest-scoring repositories every five steps and score each by the mean of its evaluations (Section 4). Figure 6 shows why this matters. Repositories if-003 and if-004 reach the highest first score, 73.33%, at steps 3 and 4. second evaluation lowers their means to 60.00% and 66.67%. The selected repository, if-016, scores 73.33%, 66.67%, 73.33% and 73.33% across four evaluations, for mean of 71.67%. first score alone would have ranked if-003 among the best repositories even though its mean is 60.00%. 8. Related Work Figure 6 Repeated validation separates high first score from consistent performance. Red shows the best firstevaluation score on ScienceBoard and blue the best mean over repeated evaluations. Computer-use agents and interaction design. Computer-use systems differ in how they expose observations and actions, and SWE-agent showed that this agent-computer interface shapes performance (Yang et al., 2024). Agent and Agent S2 organize planning, perception, and action through engineered agent components (Agashe et al., 2025a,b), while UI-TARS learns policies for GUI interaction (Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a). Other systems add programmatic access beside GUI actions, through application APIs (Lu et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026a), code execution (Song et al., 2025a), or tool calls (Jia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025). Agent S3 and its behavior judge improve task completion by selecting among multiple rollouts (Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2025). In these systems, code and tools, when available, are one action among predefined set. Agents that act only by writing and running code can outperform agents that choose from predefined actions (Lu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024). These interfaces are designed by people or written within single task. Agent S4 instead evolves them across tasks and retains the resulting operations and usage knowledge in repository that can be developed beyond the task that motivated change. Skills, memory, and tool construction. Reflexion stores textual feedback for later attempts (Shinn et al., 2023), and Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable procedures from experience (Wang et al., 2025b). Reuse can also take executable form. LLMs as Tool Makers separates tool construction from subsequent tool use (Cai et al., 2024), and SkillWeaver discovers and practices web interactions to build APIs that other agents can reuse (Zheng et al., 2025). CUA-Skill instead provides an engineered library of parameterized computer-use skills and composition graphs (Chen et al., 2026). These methods establish that agents can benefit from persistent knowledge and executable tools. Our search operates over complete repository versions containing interfaces, observation routines, configuration, and usage knowledge. Mutation and crossover can change these components together, with selection based on their combined effect on task-agent performance. 14 Evolving Agent Interfaces Automated agent design and evolutionary search. ADAS searches for agent designs expressed in code (Hu et al., 2025), and the Darwin Gödel Machine modifies its own coding agent while maintaining an archive of alternatives (Zhang et al., 2025). Self-Harness studies execution traces, proposes harness changes, and validates them through regression tests (Zhang et al., 2026b). AlphaEvolve and ShinkaEvolve combine model-generated code changes with evolutionary search and executable evaluation (Lange et al., 2025; Novikov et al., 2025), while GEPA uses trajectory reflection to evolve prompts and combine complementary improvements (Agrawal et al., 2025). Validation-based control of overfitting also predates language-model agents, including evolutionary curtailment in genetic programming (Fitzgerald and Ryan, 2011). Agent S4 evolves repositories of interfaces and knowledge through population-based search with asymmetric access to evaluation evidence. The meta-agent studies synthetic-task trajectories without ground-truth success labels and implements changes to application-specific operations, capability descriptions, and reusable workflows. The fixed harness retains control of model invocation, execution, permissions, and budgets. Keeping capabilities in the repository makes them available for revision, selection, recombination, and reuse with compatible agents and harnesses. Validation tasks, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain with the controller and are hidden from the meta-agent. Held-out performance determines which variants become parents, applying selection pressure beyond the tasks used to construct the software. 9. Conclusion We presented Agent S4, which treats interface design as an agent capability: meta-agent studies computer-use trajectories to construct and evolve reusable interfaces and knowledge about when and how to use them. The experience used for interface construction comes entirely from synthetic tasks, without ground-truth success labels or task verifiers; separate held-out validation guides repository selection. Qwen3.8-27B with repository of interfaces evolved by Agent S4 reaches 21.3% binary success on the full 108-task OSWorld V2 benchmark, above both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their reported task-solving costs. On the full 169-task ScienceBoard benchmark, separate evolution run reaches 58.58% success, compared with 41.4% for Qwen CUA. Repository and trajectory analyses show how evolution constructs application interfaces and refines the operations and observations available to subsequent task agents. These findings support learning interfaces from synthetic experience as way to improve computer use while keeping the task agents model and harness fixed, complementary to advances in both.

Evolving Agent Interfaces A. Experimental Design A.1. Benchmark Detail OSWorld V2. OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026) evaluates computer-use agents on 108 long-horizon workflows spanning everyday and professional activities in real desktop and web applications. Tasks require agents to combine information across sources, track application state, and adapt to changes during execution. The benchmark reports both binary task completion and partial scores, measuring whether agents can complete an entire workflow and how much of its requirements they satisfy. We use it as our primary benchmark for evaluating repository evolution on complex computer-use tasks. ScienceBoard. ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025) evaluates autonomous agents in realistic scientific workflows involving professional software. It contains 169 human-curated tasks across scientific domains such as biochemistry, astronomy, and geoinformatics. These tasks combine scientific reasoning with software operation through graphical and command-line interfaces, testing whether agents can translate domain-specific instructions into successful execution in scientific environments. We use ScienceBoard to evaluate whether repository evolution extends to specialized scientific applications. A.2. Settings Task subsets. The four evolution runs and their construction budgets are summarized in Table 1. OSWorld V2 uses all 30 authored synthetic tasks. ScienceBoard uses 48 of the 50 authored tasks: we exclude sb_grassgis_010, whose initialization fails region check, and sb_chimerax_006, whose input file fails to open in ChimeraX. These exclusions concern task initialization, before taskagent execution. Each benchmark uses 15 official tasks for validation. The full reported sets contain 108 OSWorld V2 tasks and 169 ScienceBoard tasks, including those validation tasks. Comparison interfaces and harnesses. The interface column in Table 2 describes the execution access exposed to the task agent. All external reference results use the OSWorld V2 reference harness with screenshot observations and 500-step budget (Yuan et al., 2026, Section 3.1). Claude Opus and Sonnet use the native Claude computer-use interface; GPT-5.5, MiniMax M3, Kimi K2.6, and Qwen3.7-Plus use the benchmarks PyAutoGUI action backend. The released GPT and MiniMax adapters translate structured computer actions into PyAutoGUI commands; this backend does not imply an unrestricted Python execution tool.3 The paper establishes the action backend for Kimi K2.6 and Qwen3.7-Plus, but the public sources do not establish their exact scored-run adapters. We label these reference interfaces Fixed: their requests and observations are set before the task. This describes the interaction surface, not prohibition on running programs through desktop applications; such programs are entered through the GUI and their output is observed in screenshots. Our Qwen CUA baseline uses the upstream Qwen harness, with structured computer_use actions for mouse, keyboard, and screenshot control translated into PyAutoGUI. Our Prime Agent conditions instead expose persistent IPython execution, supporting Python and shell code for GUI, file, and API operations. We label these interfaces Extensible: programs the agent writes during task become additional interfaces whose output returns directly to the agent. The seed and evolved conditions add repository interfaces accessible through this same tool, as described below. Harness. For our OSWorld V2 and ScienceBoard repository-evolution experiments, we use modified harness based on Prime Agent version 0.8.0-beta.546.1.a9b5d88,4 an IPython-backed coding 3Released GPT and MiniMax adapters in the benchmarks v2026.06.24 release. These establish available adapter behavior, rather than exact launch configurations for every reported model version. 4https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/releases Evolving Agent Interfaces agent. The harness prompts are reproduced in Appendix C. The model issues tool calls containing Python code, which the harness executes in persistent IPython kernel and returns the execution outputs to the model for the next step. Variables, imports, and function definitions persist across calls, allowing the agent to reuse intermediate results and invoke repository interfaces throughout task.
